newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Acer's Philippine unit born in earthquake.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Acer's Philippine unit born in earthquake.

text.p: When a massive earthquake in Japan reduced the city of Kobe to rubble three years ago, the shocks were felt in the Taipei headquarters of Acer Inc.
At the time, the Taiwanese computer giant produced all of the motherboards for its worldwide requirements in Taiwan.

"When the Japan earthquake happened, we thought what would happen if something like this happened in Taiwan. We would be finished in one night," Stone Shih, finance manager of Acer Information Products (Philippines) Inc, said.
The search for an alternate production site close to Acer's headquarters that was cost-effective and open to new investments brought Acer to the Subic Bay Freeport in the Philippines.
The freeport was set up by the Philippine government in 1992 at the site of a former U.S. naval base.

The Americans left after the Philippine Senate refused to renew leases on U.S. bases. But the longtime U.S. military presence meant that they left behind a site with good infrastructure as well as a nearly 50,000-strong workforce of trained Filipinos.
"The reason we came here was because it is just two hours from Taiwan and because of cheap labour," Shih said.
Acer set up its factory last year in a large shed that was used by the Americans as a food warehouse.
"The giant freezer is still there in the corner," Shih said as he showed visitors an assembly line where rows upon rows of young women in white uniforms added parts to computer boards.
Acer Philippines, whose exports last year exceeded $100 million, assembles 150,000 motherboards per month compared to the 220,000 per month produced by the parent firm in Taiwan.
Shih said Acer Philippines was gradually increasing its sourcing of components away from the parent.
"In future, we have to operate independent of the parent company," he said, adding that components would be sourced from the Philippines as well as other countries.
Most of the output from Acer Philippines would go to Acer subsidiaries worldwide, though a small percentage would be sold outside the Acer family of companies, he said.
Acer initially invested about $15 million in its Subic Bay facilities but the Philippine unit is still posting losses because of the launch of a massive expansion.
Over the next few years, Acer will spend at least another $70 million to build three new factories, each capable of producing 300,000 motherboards a month.
"But we will not use all three factories to make motherboards. We may use one factory to make motherboards while other factories may be used for other products," Shih said.

The new factories, two of which will be operational by the end of 1997, will be near Acer's existing facilities in the Subic Bay Taiwanese Industrial Park, a joint venture between the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority and Taiwanese developers China Development Corporation and Century Development Corporation.

At present, Acer Philippines is restricted to assembling motherboards and not finished products, such as desktop personal computers and notebook computers, because of the time-sensitive nature of the business, Shih said. Such finished products are assembled nearer to consumer markets.

New computers were coming into the market at such a fast pace that the life cycle of a product was just six months, he said. "If you push a product with the wrong timing, no one will buy it even if it is good quality at a lower price."
Moreover, if Acer Philippines made whole computers, the higher cost of transporting the larger products to market would require that they be sent by ship, Shih said.
"And by the time the ship (arrives), the market may have changed... that's why we send motherboards by air, so it is fresh like McDonalds."
